sections.html:
Avon is a town in eastern Hendricks County, Indiana, just west of Indianapolis, spread across Washington and Lincoln townships. Brownsburg borders it on the north, Danville (the county seat) lies to the west, Plainfield to the south, and Marion County to the east. Downtown Indianapolis is about 13 miles away and Danville about 7 miles.

U.S. Route 36 runs east to west through town. The old State Road 267 crossed it in the center of Avon until it was decommissioned in 2013, and that stretch is now Avon Avenue. Avon is part of the Indianapolis metropolitan area.

Avon roughly doubled in the 2000s and grew by nearly three quarters again in the 2010s. Settlement began around 1830, but the town was not incorporated until 1995.

The 2020 census found 7,781 households, 38 percent of them with children under 18, and a median age of 37.4. The town's building office publishes a list of subdivision zoning classifications, which helps when you need to know the rules for a particular street.

Newer houses nearby set the standard a buyer measures yours against, so the condition of your house and what you disclose about it count heavily.

sections.h2: Property tax for an Avon house
sections.html:
Hendricks County does the billing for Avon, so its treasurer, auditor and assessor take care of payment, deductions and assessment. Ask the county treasurer for the current due dates before you plan around any general rule.

Indiana caps what an owner pays as a share of gross assessed value. A homestead is limited to 1 percent, other residential property to 2 percent and commercial property to 3 percent, and the auditor applies a credit when the calculated tax runs above the cap.

An assessment can be appealed on Form 130, filed with the assessing official, usually by June 15 for a current-year assessment. If the informal meeting fails, the county board must hold a hearing within 180 days, and a further appeal goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 within 45 days.

The 2025 reform known as SEA 1 phases down the $48,000 standard deduction after 2026 and adds a homestead credit of 10 percent of the bill, up to $300, from 2026. A bill can move in either direction, so ask the county for the current statement before a closing.

Most of the town is in Avon Community School Corporation, whose mascot is the Oriole. The district runs Avon High School, three middle schools called North, South and West, eight elementary schools and the White Oak Early Learning Center, and it shares Harris Academy with Brownsburg Community School Corporation. Small parts of Avon fall in the Brownsburg district.

Private options include Kingsway Christian School and Our Shepherd Lutheran School, and the Avon-Washington Township Public Library serves the town. Buyers of family houses often ask which district a parcel sits in, so check the address before you answer.

Permits, inspections and zoning are handled at the Town of Avon's building department, 6570 East US Highway 36, Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. It closes daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. The phone is 317-272-0948.

  • Permit applications include building, fence and sign.
  • Inspections are scheduled through a contractor portal that requires an access code.
  • A building permit fee schedule was updated in August 2026, and cashier's checks and credit cards are the accepted payments.
  • Fence standards and sign rules sit in the municipal code.

Call the department if rental registration or a certificate of occupancy could apply to your house. Unpermitted work, such as a deck or a fence, draws questions from a buyer's inspector, and an as-is sale lets the buyer take on that cleanup.

The Town of Avon posts agendas, minutes and a document center online, and residents can subscribe to alerts on roadwork, events and local news. The Avon Redevelopment Authority and the Redevelopment Commission also hold public meetings, which shows how often public bodies take up land and project items.

The town office is at 6570 East US Highway 36 and keeps the same hours as the building department. Because Avon spans two townships and sits beside Marion County, a road project or a new development nearby can change how a buyer sees a street. Checking these postings is a simple way to know what is coming before you set a price.

sections.h2: Taxes and paperwork at an Avon closing
sections.html:
Because Hendricks County bills the tax, your first stop is the county treasurer. Ask which installment is paid, what is still open, and what the next bill is expected to be. The auditor can tell you whether a homestead deduction is on the parcel and what happens to it when the deed changes hands.

Next, take a look at the house against the building department's records. Open permits, a deck built without one, or a fence that does not meet the municipal code are the sort of items that turn up in a buyer's inspection. You do not need to fix them before a cash sale, but you should say so up front so the offer reflects the real condition.

If you belong to a homeowners association, request its rules and any dues balance. Associations commonly want a payoff statement before closing, and the title company will ask for one. Having it ready shortens the timeline.

sections.h2: What to check before choosing a sale route
sections.html:
A seller in a growing town usually has a few buyer options, and the right one depends on condition, timing and cost. Start with these checks:

  • Your homeowners association rules, if the house is in a subdivision with one.
  • Open permits or unpermitted work with the building department.
  • The latest tax bill and any open installment.
  • Whether the mortgage payoff leaves anything after costs.

Listing exposes a house to the widest group of buyers but means showings and negotiation. Selling directly to a cash buyer is faster and carries less risk of a deal falling through, since no lender appraisal or loan approval stands in the way.

With a cash sale you describe the house, review our offer and, if you accept, choose a closing date with a local title company. The title company pays off your mortgage and any open tax from the proceeds and records the deed. You do not stage, repaint or hold open houses, and you can leave behind what you do not want to move.

Whichever route you take, ask for the numbers in writing: the price, who pays each closing fee, and the date money reaches you. Then compare the written offer with what a listing would leave you after repairs, commissions and the months a house can sit.

faqs.q: What county is Avon, Indiana in?
faqs.a: Avon is in Hendricks County, whose seat is Danville. The town sits in eastern Hendricks County, west of Indianapolis.
In 1995, although settlement began around 1830. Population grew from 6,248 in 2000 to 21,474 in 2020.

faqs.a: At 6570 East US Highway 36, Avon, IN 46123. Call 317-272-0948; hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a closing from 11:30 to 12:30.
Most of the town is in Avon Community School Corporation. Small parts of Avon fall in the Brownsburg district, so check the specific address.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal an Avon property tax assessment?
faqs.a: For a current-year real property assessment, Form 130 is generally due by June 15, depending on when the notice was mailed. File it with the assessing official.
